title: The sister who saw first
hook: his older sister, Bebe Nanaki, is remembered as the first to recognize who her brother was

segments.voice: Yesterday: born at Talwandi, 1469, a baby in an ordinary village. Your line was every story starts somewhere small. Whose birthplace did you ask about? Day twenty-three.

Before the grades, before the job, before any good decisions, there is sometimes one person who believes in a child anyway. A grandmother who says this one will be something. A teacher who spots what a shy kid won't show. An older sibling who tells the others to leave the little one alone. The thank-you to people like that often goes unsaid. In the story of Guru Nanak, that person was his big sister. While the grown-ups in the village worried about the strange, dreamy boy who asked too many questions, she watched him with a different kind of attention. Today: the sister who saw first.
screen: `BEFORE THE GRADES, BEFORE THE JOB.` → `ONE PERSON BELIEVES ANYWAY.` → `FOR NANAK, HIS BIG SISTER.`

segments.voice: Her name was Nanaki, and Sikhs call her Bebe Nanaki, bebe being an affectionate word for an older sister or a respected woman. Tradition says she was about five years older than Nanak. In the janamsakhis, the young Nanak is a puzzle to the people around him. He gives things away. He sits silent for hours. He asks the village priest and teacher questions they can't answer. His father, Mehta Kalu, loved him and worried about him constantly: how would this boy ever earn a living? Nanaki saw it differently. Sikh tradition remembers her as the first to recognize that her brother wasn't lost. He was found, in a way the others couldn't see yet. Some Sikhs go so far as to call her the first Sikh, the first follower of the Guru, though she was his sister before she was anything else. And she didn't only believe in him. She did something about it. Nanaki married a man named Jai Ram and moved to the town of Sultanpur, and when her brother was a young man, drifting and at odds with his father, she brought him there. Jai Ram helped find him work, and Nanak lived near her for years. The turning point of his life, which we'll reach in a few days, happened in Sultanpur, because she made room for him there. The sources don't tell us much about her own inner life, and it's worth saying so. What they do remember is the shape of her love: she saw him first, and she made space for what she saw.
screen: `BEBE NANAKI, THE OLDER SISTER.` · `A PUZZLE TO THE GROWN-UPS.` · `SHE SAW HE WASN'T LOST.` · `SHE MADE ROOM IN SULTANPUR.` · then, large: `SOMEONE SAW YOU FIRST.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let a face come to mind: someone who believed in you early, before there was much evidence. Picture them clearly, their voice, a thing they said. Remember a moment when their faith in you made a difference. Let yourself feel grateful, fully, without rushing. And if you can, think about what you'd say to them now, if you could say one sentence. Hold that sentence. The bell holds the time.
Bebe Nanaki. Guru Nanak's older sister, remembered as the first to recognize who her brother was, and who made room for him to become it.
Your line: someone saw you first. Today, send that one sentence to the person who believed in you early. If they're gone, say it out loud anyway. Day twenty-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs honor Bebe Nanaki as Guru Nanak's devoted older sister, often called the first to recognize him; a gurdwara in her memory stands in Sultanpur Lodhi.
